entries.fcc1bed740cd01f715937bd224bccc7f5d7f6666: <div sID="gen3921" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="31" osisID="Deut.31" sID="Deut.31"/> <div eID="gen3921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3922" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3923" type="x-p"/> In this chapter Moses, having finished his sermon, I. Encourages both the people who were now to enter Canaan (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.1-Deut.31.6">ver. 1-6</reference>), and Joshua who was to lead them, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.7-Deut.31.8">ver. 7, 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.23">23</reference>. And, II. He takes care for the keeping of these things always in their remembrance after his decease, 1. By the book of the law which was, (1.) Written. (2.) Delivered into the custody of the priests, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.9">ver. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.24-Deut.31.27">and 24-27</reference>. (3.) Ordered to be publicly read every seventh year, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.10-Deut.31.13">ver. 10-13</reference>. 2. By a song which God orders Moses to prepare for their instruction and admonition. (1.) He calls Moses and Joshua to the door of the tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.14-Deut.31.15">ver. 14, 15</reference>. (2.) He foretells the apostasy of Israel in process of time, and the judgments they would thereby bring upon themselves, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.16-Deut.31.18">ver. 16-18</reference>. (3.) He prescribes the following song to be a witness against them, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.19-Deut.31.21">ver. 19-21</reference>. (4.) Moses wrote it, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.22">ver. 22</reference>. And delivered it to Israel, with an intimation of the design of it, as he had received it from the Lord, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.28-Deut.31.30">ver. 28</reference>, &c.
entries.1c5b1acefb43146a0df427bf21658d71c0ba6dc1: <div eID="gen3923" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3922" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Solemn Warnings; Joshua Encouraged. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3924" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And Moses went and spake these words unto all Israel. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he said unto them, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> a hundred and twenty years old this day; I can no more go out and come in: also the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath said unto me, Thou shalt not go over this Jordan. <hi type="super">3</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, he will go over before thee, <hi type="italic">and</hi> he will destroy these nations from before thee, and thou shalt possess them: <hi type="italic">and</hi> Joshua, he shall go over before thee, as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath said. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall do unto them as he did to Sihon and to Og, kings of the Amorites, and unto the land of them, whom he destroyed. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall give them up before your face, that ye may do unto them according unto all the commandments which I have commanded you. <hi type="super">6</hi> Be strong and of a good courage, fear not, nor be afraid of them: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, he <hi type="italic">it is</hi> that doth go with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee. <hi type="super">7</hi> And Moses called unto Joshua, and said unto him in the sight of all Israel, Be strong and of a good courage: for thou must go with this people unto the land which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath sworn unto their fathers to give them; and thou shalt cause them to inherit it. <hi type="super">8</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , he <hi type="italic">it is</hi> that doth go before thee; he will be with thee, he will not fail thee, neither forsake thee: fear not, neither be dismayed. <div eID="gen3924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3925" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Loth to part</hi> (we say) <hi type="italic">bids oft farewell.</hi> Moses does so to the children of Israel: not because he was loth to go to God, but because he was loth to leave them, fearing that when he had left them they would leave God. He had finished what he had to say to them by way of counsel and exhortation: here he calls them together to give them a word of encouragement, especially with reference to the wars of Canaan, in which they were now to engage. It was a discouragement to them that Moses was to be removed at a time when he could so ill be spared: though Joshua was continued to fight for them in the valley, they would want Moses to intercede for them on the hill, as he did, <reference osisRef="Exod.17.10">Exod. xvii. 10</reference>. But there is no remedy: <hi type="italic">Moses can no more go out and come in,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.31.2">v. 2</reference>. Not that he was disabled by any decay either of body or mind; for his <hi type="italic">natural force was not abated,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.24.7">ch. xxiv. 7</reference>. But he cannot any longer discharge his office; for, 1. He is 120 <hi type="italic">years old,</hi> and it is time for him to think of resigning his honour and returning to his rest. He that had arrived at so great an age then, when seventy or eighty was the ordinary stint, as appears by the prayer of Moses (<reference osisRef="Ps.90.10">Ps. xc. 10</reference>), might well think that he had accomplished as a hireling his day. 2. He is under a divine sentence: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not go over Jordan.</hi> Thus a full stop was put to his usefulness; hitherto he must go, hitherto he must serve, but no further. So God had appointed it and Moses acquiesces: for I know not why we should any of us desire to live a day longer than while God has work for us to do; nor shall we be accountable for more time than is allotted us. But, though Moses must not go over himself, he is anxious to encourage those that must. <div eID="gen3925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3926" type="x-p"/> I. He encourages the people; and never could any general animate his soldiers upon such good grounds as those on which Moses here encourages Israel. 1. He assures them of the constant presence of God with them (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord thy God.</hi> that has led thee and kept thee hitherto <hi type="italic">will go over before thee;</hi> and those might follow boldly who were sure that they had God for their leader. He repeats it again (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.6">v. 6</reference>) with an emphasis: "<hi type="italic">The Lord thy God,</hi> the great Jehovah, who is thine in covenant, <hi type="italic">he it is,</hi> he and no less, he and no other, <hi type="italic">that goes before thee;</hi> not only who by his promise has assured thee that he <hi type="italic">will go before thee;</hi> but by his ark, the visible token of his presence, shows thee that he <hi type="italic">does</hi> actually <hi type="italic">go before thee.</hi>" And he repeats it with enlargement: "Not only he goes over before thee at first, to bring thee in, but he will continue with thee all along, with thee and thine; <hi type="italic">he will not fail thee nor forsake thee;</hi> he will not disappoint thy expectations in any strait, nor will he ever desert thy interest; be constant to him, and he will be so to thee." This is applied by the apostle to all God's spiritual Israel, for the encouragement of their faith and hope; unto us is this gospel preached, as well as unto them <hi type="italic">He will never fail thee, nor forsake thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.5">Heb. xiii. 5</reference>. 2. He commends Joshua to them for a leader: <hi type="italic">Joshua, he shall go over before thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.31.3">v. 3</reference>. One whose conduct, and courage, and sincere affection to their interest, they had had long experience of; and one whom God had ordained and appointed to be their leader, and therefore, no doubt, would own and bless, and make a blessing to them. See <reference osisRef="Num.27.18">Num. xxvii. 18</reference>. Note, It is a great encouragement to a people when, instead of some useful instruments that are removed, God raises up others to carry on his work. 3. He ensures their success. The greatest generals, supported with the greatest advantages, must yet own the issues of war to be doubtful and uncertain; the battle is not always to the strong nor to the bold; an ill accident unthought of may turn the scale against the highest hopes. But Moses had warrant from God to assure Israel that, notwithstanding the disadvantages they laboured under, they should certainly be victorious. A coward will fight when he is sure to be a conqueror. God undertakes to do the work—<hi type="italic">he will destroy these nations;</hi> and Israel shall do little else than divide the spoil—<hi type="italic">thou shalt possess them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.31.3">v. 3</reference>. Two things might encourage their hopes of this:—(1.) The victories they had already obtained over Sihon and Og (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.4">v. 4</reference>), from which they might infer both the power of God, that he could do what he had done, and the purpose of God, that he would finish what he had begun to do. Thus must we improve our experience. (2.) The command God had given them to destroy the Canaanites (<reference osisRef="Deut.7.2">ch. vii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.12.2">xii. 2</reference>), to which he refers here (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.5">v. 5</reference>, that you <hi type="italic">may do unto them according to all which I have commanded you</hi>), and from which they might infer that, if God had commanded them to destroy the Canaanites, no doubt he would put it into the power of their hands to do it. Note, What God has made our duty we have reason to expect opportunity and assistance from him for the doing of. So that from all this he had reason enough to bid them <hi type="italic">be strong and of a good courage,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.31.6">v. 6</reference>. While they had the power of God engaged for them they had no reason to fear all the powers of Canaan engaged against them. <div eID="gen3926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3927" type="x-p"/> II. He encourages Joshua, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.7-Deut.31.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. Observe, 1. Though Joshua was an experienced general, and a man of approved gallantry and resolution, who had already signalized himself in many brave actions, yet Moses saw cause to bid him <hi type="italic">be of good courage,</hi> now that he was entering upon a new scene of action; and Joshua was far from taking it as an affront, or as a tacit questioning of his courage, to be thus charged, as sometimes we find proud and peevish spirits invidiously taking exhortations and admonitions for reproaches and reflections. Joshua himself is very well pleased to be admonished by Moses to be strong and of good courage. 2. He gives him this charge <hi type="italic">in the sight of all Israel,</hi> that they might be the more observant of him whom they saw thus solemnly inaugurated, and that he might set himself the more to be an example of courage to the people who were witnesses to this charge here given to him as well as to themselves. 3. He gives him the same assurances of the divine presence, and consequently of a glorious success, that he had given the people. God would be with him, would not forsake him, and therefore he should certainly accomplish the glorious enterprise to which he was called and commissioned: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt cause them to inherit the land</hi> of promise. Note, Those shall speed well that have God with them; and therefore they ought to <hi type="italic">be of good courage.</hi> Through God let us do valiantly, for through him we shall do victoriously; if we resist the devil, he shall flee, and God shall <hi type="italic">shortly tread him under our feet.</hi>
entries.cac9e48fe3b9e48c3afb4ea58d8fe8a6e41ef7dc: <div eID="gen3927" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Reading of the Law. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3928" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And Moses wrote this law, and delivered it unto the priests the sons of Levi, which bare the ark of the covenant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and unto all the elders of Israel. <hi type="super">10</hi> And Moses commanded them, saying, At the end of <hi type="italic">every</hi> seven years, in the solemnity of the year of release, in the feast of tabernacles, <hi type="super">11</hi> When all Israel is come to appear before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God in the place which he shall choose, thou shalt read this law before all Israel in their hearing. <hi type="super">12</hi> Gather the people together, men, and women, and children, and thy stranger that <hi type="italic">is</hi> within thy gates, that they may hear, and that they may learn, and fear the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, and observe to do all the words of this law: <hi type="super">13</hi> And <hi type="italic">that</hi> their children, which have not known <hi type="italic">any thing,</hi> may hear, and learn to fear the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, as long as ye live in the land whither ye go over Jordan to possess it. <div eID="gen3928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3929" type="x-p"/> The law was given by Moses; so it is said, <reference osisRef="John.1.17">John i. 17</reference>. He was not only entrusted to deliver it to that generation, but to transmit it to the generations to come; and here it appears that he was faithful to that trust. <div eID="gen3929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3930" type="x-p"/> I. <hi type="italic">Moses wrote this law,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.31.9">v. 9</reference>. The learned bishop Patrick understands this of all the five books of Moses, which are often called the <hi type="italic">law;</hi> he supposes that though Moses had written most of the Pentateuch before, yet he did not finish it till now; now he put his last hand to that sacred volume. Many think that the law here (especially since it is called <hi type="italic">this law,</hi> this grand abridgment of the law) is to be understood of this book of Deuteronomy; all those discourses to the people which have taken up this whole book, he, being in them divinely inspired, wrote them as the word of God. He wrote this law, 1. That those who had heard it might often review it themselves, and call it to mind. 2. That it might be the more safely handed down to posterity. Note, The church has received abundance of advantage from the writing, as well as from the preaching, of divine things; faith comes not only by hearing, but by reading. The same care that was taken of the law, thanks be to God, is taken of the gospel too; soon after it was preached it was written, that it might reach to those on whom the ends of the world shall come. <div eID="gen3930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3931" type="x-p"/> II. Having written it, he committed it to the care and custody of the priests and elders. He delivered one authentic copy to the priests, to be laid up by the ark (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.26">v. 26</reference>), there to remain as a standard by which all other copies must be tried. And it is supposed that he gave another copy to the elders of each tribe, to be transcribed by all of that tribe that were so disposed. Some observe that the elders, as well as the priests, were entrusted with the law, to intimate that magistrates by the power, as well as ministers by their doctrine, are to maintain religion, and to take care that the law be not broken nor lost. <div eID="gen3931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3932" type="x-p"/> III. He appointed the public reading of this law in a general assembly of all Israel every seventh year. The pious Jews (it is very probable) read the laws daily in their families, and <hi type="italic">Moses of old time was read in the synagogue every sabbath day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.15.21">Acts xv. 21</reference>. But once in seven years, that the law might be the more magnified and made honourable, it must be read in a general assembly. Though we read the word in private, we must not think it needless to hear it read in public. Now here he give direction, <div eID="gen3932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3933" type="x-p"/> 1. When this solemn reading of the law must be, that the time might add to the solemnity; it must be done, (1.) In the year of release. In that year the land rested, so that they could the better spare time to attend this service. Servants who were then discharged, and poor debtors who were then acquitted from their debts, must know that, having the benefit of the law, it was justly expected they should yield obedience to it, and therefore give up themselves to be God's servants, because he had loosed their bonds. The year of release was typical of gospel grace, which therefore is called the <hi type="italic">acceptable year of the Lord;</hi> for our remission and liberty by Christ engage us to keep his commandments, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.74-Luke.1.75">Luke i. 74, 75</reference>. (2.) At the feast of tabernacles in that year. In that feast they were particularly required to <hi type="italic">rejoice before God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.23.40">Lev. xxiii. 40</reference>. Therefore then they must read the law, both to qualify their mirth and keep it in due bounds, and to sanctify their mirth, that they might make the law of God the matter of their rejoicing, and might read it with pleasure and not as a task. <div eID="gen3933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3934" type="x-p"/> 2. To whom it must be read: To <hi type="italic">all Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.11">v. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">men, women, and children, and the strangers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.31.12">v. 12</reference>. The women and children were not obliged to go up to the other feasts, but to this only in which the law was read. Note, It is the will of God that all people should acquaint themselves with his word. It is a rule to all, and therefore should be read to all. It is supposed that, since all Israel could not possibly meet in one place, nor could one man's voice reach them all, as many as the courts of the Lord's house would hold met there, and the rest at the same time in their synagogues. The Jewish doctors say that the hearers were bound to <hi type="italic">prepare their hearts,</hi> and to hear <hi type="italic">with fear and reverence, and with joy and trembling,</hi> as in the day <hi type="italic">when the law was given on Mount Sinai;</hi> and, though there were <hi type="italic">great and wise men who knew the whole law very well,</hi> yet they were bound to <hi type="italic">hear with great attention;</hi> for he that <hi type="italic">reads is the messenger of the congregation to cause the words of God to be heard.</hi> I wish those that hear the gospel read and preached would consider this. <div eID="gen3934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3935" type="x-p"/> 3. By whom it must be read: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt read it</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.11">v. 11</reference>), "Thou, O Israel," by a proper person appointed for that purpose; or, "Thou, O Joshua," their chief ruler; accordingly we find that he did read the law himself, <reference osisRef="Josh.8.34-Josh.8.35">Josh. viii. 34, 35</reference>. So did Josiah, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.30">2 Chron. xxxiv. 30</reference>, and Ezra, <reference osisRef="Neh.8.3">Neh. viii. 3</reference>. And the Jews say that the king himself (when they had one) was the person that read in the courts of the temple, that a pulpit was set up for that purpose in the midst of the court, in which the king stood, that the book of the law was delivered to him by the high priest, that he stood up to receive it, uttered a prayer (as every one did that was to read the law in public) before he read; and then, if he pleased, he might sit down and read. But if he read standing it was thought the more commendable, as (they say) king Agrippa did. Here let me offer it as a conjecture that Solomon is called the <hi type="italic">preacher,</hi> in his Ecclesiastes, because he delivered the substance of that book in a discourse to the people, after his public reading of the law in the feast of tabernacles, according to this appointment here. <div eID="gen3935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3936" type="x-p"/> 4. For what end it must be thus solemnly read. (1.) That the present generation might hereby keep up their acquaintance with the law of God, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.12">v. 12</reference>. They must hear, that they may learn, and <hi type="italic">fear God, and observe to do their duty.</hi> See here what we are to aim at in hearing the word; we must hear, that we may learn and grow in knowledge; and every time we read the scriptures we shall find that there is still more and more to be learned out of them. We must learn, that we may fear God, that is, that we may be duly affected with divine things; and must fear God, that we may <hi type="italic">observe and do the words of his law;</hi> for in vain do we pretend to fear him if we do not obey him. (2.) That the rising generation might betimes be leavened with religion (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.13">v. 13</reference>); not only that those who know something may thus know more, but that <hi type="italic">the children who have not known any thing</hi> may betimes know this, how much it is their interest as well as duty to fear God.
entries.c5578471ce264e717c22067b224a4396974c361a: <div eID="gen3936" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Apostasy Foretold. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3937" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, Behold, thy days approach that thou must die: call Joshua, and present yourselves in the tabernacle of the congregation, that I may give him a charge. And Moses and Joshua went, and presented themselves in the tabernacle of the congregation. <hi type="super">15</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> appeared in the tabernacle in a pillar of a cloud: and the pillar of the cloud stood over the door of the tabernacle. <hi type="super">16</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Moses, Behold, thou shalt sleep with thy fathers; and this people will rise up, and go a whoring after the gods of the strangers of the land, whither they go <hi type="italic">to be</hi> among them, and will forsake me, and break my covenant which I have made with them. <hi type="super">17</hi> Then my anger shall be kindled against them in that day, and I will forsake them, and I will hide my face from them, and they shall be devoured, and many evils and troubles shall befall them; so that they will say in that day, Are not these evils come upon us, because our God <hi type="italic">is</hi> not among us? <hi type="super">18</hi> And I will surely hide my face in that day for all the evils which they shall have wrought, in that they are turned unto other gods. <hi type="super">19</hi> Now therefore write ye this song for you, and teach it the children of Israel: put it in their mouths, that this song may be a witness for me against the children of Israel. <hi type="super">20</hi> For when I shall have brought them into the land which I sware unto their fathers, that floweth with milk and honey; and they shall have eaten and filled themselves, and waxen fat; then will they turn unto other gods, and serve them, and provoke me, and break my covenant. <hi type="super">21</hi> And it shall come to pass, when many evils and troubles are befallen them, that this song shall testify against them as a witness; for it shall not be forgotten out of the mouths of their seed: for I know their imagination which they go about, even now, before I have brought them into the land which I sware. <div eID="gen3937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3938" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Moses and Joshua are summoned to attend the divine majesty at the door of the tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.14">v. 14</reference>. Moses is told again that he must shortly die; even those that are most ready and willing to die have need to be often reminded of the approach of death. In consideration of this, he must come himself to meet God; for whatever improves our communion with God furthers our preparation for death. He must also bring Joshua with him to be presented to God for a successor, and to receive his commission and charge. Moses readily obeys the summons, for he was not one of those that look with an evil eye upon their successors, but, on the contrary, rejoiced in him. <div eID="gen3938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3939" type="x-p"/> II. God graciously gives them the meeting: <hi type="italic">He appeared in the tabernacle</hi> (as the shechinah used to appear) <hi type="italic">in a pillar of a cloud,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.31.15">v. 15</reference>. This is the only time in all this book that we read of the glory of God appearing, whereas we often read of it in the three foregoing books, which perhaps signifies that in the latter days, under the evangelical law, such visible appearances as these of the divine glory are not to be expected, but we must take heed to the more sure word of prophecy. <div eID="gen3939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3940" type="x-p"/> III. He tells Moses that, after his death, the covenant which he had taken so much pains to make between Israel and their God would certainly be broken. 1. That Israel would <hi type="italic">forsake God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.31.16">v. 16</reference>. And we may be sure that if the covenant between God and man be broken the blame must lie on man, it is he that breaks it; we have often observed it, That God never leaves any till they first leave him. Worshipping the gods of the Canaanites (who had been the natives, but henceforward were to be looked upon as the strangers of that land) would undoubtedly be counted a deserting of God, and, like adultery, a violation of the covenant. Thus still those are revolters from Christ, and will be so adjudged, who either make a god of their money by reigning covetousness or a god of their belly by reigning sensuality. Those that <hi type="italic">turn to other gods</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.18">v. 18</reference>) forsake their own mercies. This apostasy of theirs is foretold to be the effect of their prosperity (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall have eaten and filled themselves;</hi> this is all they will aim at in eating, to gratify their own appetites, and then they will wax fat, grow secure and sensual; their security will take off their dread of God and his judgments; and their sensuality will incline them to the idolatries of the heathen, which <hi type="italic">made provision for the flesh to fulfil the lusts of it.</hi> Note, God has a clear and infallible foresight of all the wickedness of the wicked, and has often covenanted with those who <hi type="italic">he knew would deal very treacherously</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.8">Isa. xlviii. 8</reference>), and conferred many favours on those who he knew would deal very ungratefully. 2. That then God would forsake Israel; and justly does he cast those off who had so unjustly cast him off (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">My anger shall be kindled against them, and I will forsake them.</hi> His providence would forsake them, no longer to protect and prosper them, and then they would become a prey to all their neighbours. His spirit and grace would forsake them, no longer to teach and guide them, and then they would be more and more bigoted, besotted, and hardened in their idolatries. Thus <hi type="italic">many evils and troubles would befal them.</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.17">v. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.21">21</reference>), which would be such manifest indications of God's displeasure against them that they themselves would be constrained to own it: <hi type="italic">Have not these evils come upon us because our God is not among us?</hi> Those that have sinned away their God will find that thereby they pull all mischiefs upon their own heads. But that which completed their misery was that God would <hi type="italic">hide his face from them in that day,</hi> that day of their trouble and distress, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.18">v. 18</reference>. Whatever outward troubles we are in, if we have but the light of God's countenance, we may be easy. But, if God hide his face from us and our prayers, we are undone. <div eID="gen3940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3941" type="x-p"/> IV. He directs Moses to deliver them a song, in the composing of which he should be divinely inspired, and which should remain a standing testimony for God as faithful to them in giving them warning, and against them as persons false to themselves in not taking the warning, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.19">v. 19</reference>. The written word in general, as well as this song in particular, is a witness for God against all those that break covenant with him. It shall be for a testimony, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.14">Matt. xxiv. 14</reference>. The wisdom of man has devised many ways of conveying the knowledge of good and evil, by laws, histories, prophecies, proverbs, and, among the rest, by songs; each has its advantages. And the wisdom of God has in the scripture made use of them all, that ignorant and careless men might be left inexcusable. 1. This song, if rightly improved, might be a means to prevent their apostasy; for in the inditing of it God had an eye to their present imagination, now, <hi type="italic">before they were brought into the land of promise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.31.21">v. 21</reference>. God knew very well that there were in their hearts such gross conceits of the deity, and such inclinations of idolatry, that they would be tinder to the sparks of that temptation; and therefore in this song he gives them warning of their danger that way. Note, The word of God is a <hi type="italic">discerner of the thoughts and intents of men's hearts,</hi> and meets with them strangely by its reproofs and corrections, <reference osisRef="Heb.4.12">Heb. iv. 12</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.25">1 Cor. xiv. 25</reference>. Ministers who preach the word know not the imaginations men go about, but God, whose word it is, knows perfectly. 2. If this song did not prevent their apostasy, yet it might help to bring them to repentance, and to recover them from their apostasy. When their troubles come upon them, this <hi type="italic">song shall not be forgotten,</hi> but may serve as a glass to show them their own faces, that they may humble themselves, and return to him from whom they have revolted. Note, Those for whom God has mercy in store he may leave to fall, yet he will provide means for their recovery. Medicines are prepared before-hand for their cure.
entries.defa3ec99dd163679e5de6656143baad1cdb40cb: <div eID="gen3941" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Song of Moses. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3942" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Moses therefore wrote this song the same day, and taught it the children of Israel. <hi type="super">23</hi> And he gave Joshua the son of Nun a charge, and said, Be strong and of a good courage: for thou shalt bring the children of Israel into the land which I sware unto them: and I will be with thee. <hi type="super">24</hi> And it came to pass, when Moses had made an end of writing the words of this law in a book, until they were finished, <hi type="super">25</hi> That Moses commanded the Levites, which bare the ark of the covenant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, <hi type="super">26</hi> Take this book of the law, and put it in the side of the ark of the covenant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, that it may be there for a witness against thee. <hi type="super">27</hi> For I know thy rebellion, and thy stiff neck: behold, while I am yet alive with you this day, ye have been rebellious against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and how much more after my death? <hi type="super">28</hi> Gather unto me all the elders of your tribes, and your officers, that I may speak these words in their ears, and call heaven and earth to record against them. <hi type="super">29</hi> For I know that after my death ye will utterly corrupt <hi type="italic">yourselves,</hi> and turn aside from the way which I have commanded you; and evil will befall you in the latter days; because ye will do evil in the sight of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to provoke him to anger through the work of your hands. <hi type="super">30</hi> And Moses spake in the ears of all the congregation of Israel the words of this song, until they were ended. <div eID="gen3942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3943" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The charge is given to Joshua, which God has said (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.14">v. 14</reference>) he would give him. The same in effect that Moses had given him. The same in effect that Moses had given him (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Be strong and of a good courage,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.31.23">v. 23</reference>. Joshua had now heard from God so much of the wickedness of the people whom he was to have the conduct of as could not but be a discouragement to him: "Nay," says God, "how bad soever they are, thou shalt go through thy understanding, for <hi type="italic">I will be with thee.</hi> Thou shalt put them into possession of Canaan. If they afterwards by their sin throw themselves out of it again, that will be no fault of thine, nor any dishonour to thee, therefore <hi type="italic">be of good courage.</hi>" <div eID="gen3943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3944" type="x-p"/> II. The solemn delivery of the book of the law to the Levites, to be deposited in the side of the ark, is here again related (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.24-Deut.31.26">v. 24-26</reference>), of which before, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.9">v. 9</reference>. Only they are here directed where to treasure up this precious original, not in the ark (there only the two tables were preserved), but in another box <hi type="italic">by the side of the ark.</hi> It is probable that this was the very book that was found in the house of the Lord (having been somehow or other misplaced) in the days of Josiah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.14">2 Chron. xxxiv. 14</reference>), and so perhaps the following words here, <hi type="italic">that it may be a witness against thee,</hi> may particularly point at that event, which happened so long after; for the finding of this very book occasioned the public reading of it by Josiah himself, for a witness against a people who were then almost ripe for their ruin by the Babylonians. <div eID="gen3944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3945" type="x-p"/> III. The song which follows in the next chapter is here delivered to Moses, and by him to the people. He wrote it first (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.22">v. 22</reference>), as the Spirit of God indited it, and then <hi type="italic">spoke it in the ears of all the congregation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.30">v. 30</reference>), and taught it to them (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.22">v. 22</reference>), that is, gave out copies of it, and ordered the people to learn it by heart. It was delivered by word of mouth first, and afterwards in writing, to the elders and officers, as the representatives of their respective tribes (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.28">v. 28</reference>), by them to be transmitted to their several families and households. It was delivered to them with a solemn appeal to heaven and earth concerning the fair warning which was given them by it of the fatal consequences of their apostasy from God, and with a declaration of the little joy and little hope Moses had in and concerning them. 1. He declares what little joy he had had of them while he was with them, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.27">v. 27</reference>. It is not in a passion that he says, <hi type="italic">I know thy rebellion</hi> (as once he said unadvisedly, <hi type="italic">Hear now, you rebels</hi>), but it is the result of a long acquaintance with them: <hi type="italic">you have been rebellious against the Lord.</hi> Their rebellions against himself he makes no mention of: these he had long since forgiven and forgotten; but they must be made to hear of their rebellions against God, that they may be ever repented of and never repeated. 2. What little hopes he had of them now that he was leaving them. From what God had now said to him (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.16">v. 16</reference>) more than from his own experience of them, though that was discouraging enough, he tells them (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.29">v. 29</reference>), <hi type="italic">I know that after my death you will utterly corrupt yourselves.</hi> Many a sad thought, no doubt, it occasioned to this good man, to foresee the apostasy and ruin of a people he had taken so much pains with, in order to them good and make them happy; but this was his comfort, that he had done his duty, and that God would be glorified, if not in their settlement, yet in their dispersion. Thus our Lord Jesus, a little before his death, foretold the rise of false Christs and false prophets (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.24">Matt. xxiv. 24</reference>), notwithstanding which, and all the apostasies of the latter times, we may be confident that <hi type="italic">the gates of hell shall not prevail against the church,</hi> for the <hi type="italic">foundation of God stands sure.</hi>  <chapter eID="Deut.31"/> <div eID="gen3945" type="x-p"/>

entries.6f053ca24617fc3971142b78df2e8b6fe6d69be9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1915"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 31</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Deut.31.1-Deut.31.8">De 31:1-8</reference>. Moses Encourages the People and Joshua.</title> <div sID="gen2542" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1915"/><hi type="bold">1. Moses went and spake--</hi>It is probable that this rehearsal of the law extended over several successive days; and it might be the last and most important day on which the return of Moses to the place of assembly is specially noticed. In drawing his discourse towards a conclusion, he adverted to his advanced age; and although neither his physical nor intellectual powers had suffered any decay (<reference osisRef="Deut.34.7">De 34:7</reference>), yet he knew, by a special revelation, that the time had arrived when he was about to be withdrawn from the superintendence and government of Israel. <div eID="gen2542" type="x-p"/>
entries.d28325b8b0ee6e9eed395c23203fb5058383c934: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1916"/><div sID="gen2543" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1916"/><hi type="bold">2-8. also the Lord hath said--</hi>should be "for the Lord hath said" thou shalt not go over this Jordan. While taking a solemn leave of the people, Moses exhorted them not to be intimidated by the menacing opposition of enemies; to take encouragement from the continued presence of their covenanted God; and to rest assured that the same divine power, which had enabled them to discomfit their first assailants on the east of Jordan, would aid them not less effectually in the adventurous enterprise which they were about to undertake, and by which they would obtain possession of "the land which He had sworn unto their fathers to give them." <div eID="gen2543" type="x-p"/>
entries.082956889ccefd6a6a7bac4b696448de5e1528af: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1917"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Deut.31.9-Deut.31.13">De 31:9-13</reference>. He Delivers the Law to the Priests, to Read It Every Seventh Year to the People.</title> <div sID="gen2544" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1917"/><hi type="bold">9-13. And Moses wrote this law, and delivered it unto the priests--</hi>The law thus committed to writing was either the whole book of Deuteronomy, or the important part of it contained between the twenty-seventh and thirtieth chapters. It was usual in cases of public or private contract for two copies of the engagement to be made--one to be deposited in the national archives or some secure place for reference, should occasion require. The other was to remain in the hands of the contracting parties (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.12-Jer.32.14">Jr 32:12-14</reference>). The same course was followed on this renewal of the covenant between God and Israel. Two written copies of the law were prepared, the one of which was delivered to the public representatives of Israel; namely, the priests and the elders.<div eID="gen2544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2545" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the priests, ... who bare the ark of the covenant--</hi>In all ordinary journeys, it was the common duty of the Levites to carry the ark and its furniture (<reference osisRef="Num.4.15">Nu 4:15</reference>); but, on solemn or extraordinary occasions, that office was discharged by the priests (Jos 3:3-8; 6:<reference osisRef="Josh.8.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.11">1Ch 15:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen2545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2546" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all the elders of Israel--</hi>They were assistants to the priests and overseers to take care of the preservation, rehearsal, and observance of the law. <div eID="gen2546" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9052c078a1ac0bb666f4c7cb0d7ed7da1508390: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1919"/><div sID="gen2548" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1919"/><hi type="bold">14-15. the Lord said unto Moses, ...call Joshua, and present yourselves in the tabernacle of the congregation--</hi>Joshua had been publicly designated to the office of commander by Moses [Nu 27:22, 23]; and God was pleased to confirm his appointment by the visible symbols of His presence and approval. As none but the priests were privileged to enter the sanctuary, it is probable that this significant manifestation of the cloudy pillar was made while the leaders stood at the door of the tabernacle. <div eID="gen2548" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6b91154336f02c900df6d185adf708fe9ec3ebf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1920"/><div sID="gen2549" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1920"/><hi type="bold">16-22. the Lord said unto Moses, ... this people will rise up--</hi>In this remarkable interview, Moses was distinctly apprised of the infidelity of Israel, their corruptions of the true religion through intercourse with the idolatrous inhabitants of Canaan (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.26">Am 5:26</reference>), and their chastisements in consequence of those national defections. <div eID="gen2549" type="x-p"/>
entries.55fd416897a2de0536bf456080a0766b867432b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1923"/><div sID="gen2552" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1923"/><hi type="bold">26. Take this book of the law, and put it in the side of the ark--</hi>The second copy of the law (see on <reference osisRef="Deut.31.9">De 31:9</reference>) was deposited for greater security and reverence in a little chest beside the ark of the covenant, for there was nothing contained within it but the tables of stone (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.9">1Ki 8:9</reference>). Others think it was put within the ark, it being certain, from the testimony of Paul (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.4">He 9:4</reference>), that there were once other things inside the ark, and that this was the copy found in the time of Josiah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.8">2Ki 22:8</reference>). <chapter eID="Deut.31"/>

entries.a3ff74bf80fd1f2c95536ef00146d3b53f18bbac: <div eID="gen7117" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen7118" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7119" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7119" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7118" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7120" type="x-p"/> Moses, being one hundred and twenty years old and about to die, calls the people together, and exhorts them to courage and obedience, <reference osisRef="Deu.31.1-Deu.31.6">Deu 31:1-6</reference>. Delivers a charge to Joshua, <reference osisRef="Deu.31.7">Deu 31:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.31.8">Deu 31:8</reference>. Delivers the law which he hod written to the priests, with a solemn charge that they should read it every seventh year, publicly to all the people, <reference osisRef="Deu.31.9-Deu.31.13">Deu 31:9-13</reference>. The Lord calls Moses and Joshua to the tabernacle, <reference osisRef="Deu.31.14">Deu 31:14</reference>. He appears to them, informs Moses of his approaching death, and delivers to him a prophetical and historical song, or poem, which he is to leave with Israel, for their instruction and reproof, <reference osisRef="Deu.31.15-Deu.31.21">Deu 31:15-21</reference>. Moses writes the song the same day, and teaches it to the Israelites, <reference osisRef="Deu.31.22">Deu 31:22</reference>; gives Joshua a charge, <reference osisRef="Deu.31.23">Deu 31:23</reference>; finishes writing the book of the law, <reference osisRef="Deu.31.24">Deu 31:24</reference>. Commands the Levites to lay it up in the side of the ark, <reference osisRef="Deu.31.25">Deu 31:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.31.26">Deu 31:26</reference>. Predicts their rebellions, <reference osisRef="Deu.31.27">Deu 31:27</reference>. Orders the elders to be gathered together, and shows them what evils would befall the people in the latter days, <reference osisRef="Deu.31.28">Deu 31:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.31.29">Deu 31:29</reference>, and repeats the song to them, <reference osisRef="Deu.31.30">Deu 31:30</reference>.
entries.b60fa4336b4794c95fec9abada4dfa46dd9fb4fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen7120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7121" type="x-p"/> I am a hundred and twenty years old - The life of Moses, the great prophet of God and lawgiver of the Jews, was exactly the same in length as the time Noah employed in preaching righteousness to the antediluvian world. These one hundred and twenty years were divided into three remarkable periods: forty years he lived in Egypt, in Pharaoh's court, acquiring all the learning and wisdom of the Egyptians; (see <reference osisRef="Act.7.20">Act 7:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.7.23">Act 7:23</reference>); forty years he sojourned in the land of Midian in a state of preparation for his great and important mission; (<reference osisRef="Act.7.29">Act 7:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.7.30">Act 7:30</reference>); and forty years he guided, led, and governed the Israelites under the express direction and authority of God: in all, one hundred and twenty years.
entries.90e14e8694ef27aff27a90f1da2743f5fe9013fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen7121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7122" type="x-p"/> Joshua, he shall go over before thee - See on <reference osisRef="Num.27.17">Num 27:17</reference> (note), etc.
entries.55304ebb22ea627b81187c8a4ef37b3e81b00e23: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen7122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7123" type="x-p"/> Be strong - חזקו chizku, the same word that is used <reference osisRef="Exo.4.21">Exo 4:21</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Exo.9.15">Exo 9:15</reference> (note), for hardening Pharaoh's heart. See the notes there. The Septuagint, in this and the following verse, have, Ανδριζου και ισχυε, Play the man, and be strong; and from this St. Paul seems to have borrowed his ideas, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.13">1Cor 16:13</reference> : Στηκετε εν τῃ πιστει· ανδριζεσθε, κρατιουσθε: Stand firm in the faith; play the man - act like heroes; be vigorous.
entries.78bc49095b43186044bb837b9ff68585bee80be9: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen7123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7124" type="x-p"/> The Lord - doth go before thee - To prepare thy way, and to direct thee. <div eID="gen7124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7125" type="x-p"/> He will be with thee - Accompany thee in all thy journeys, and assist thee in all thy enterprises. <div eID="gen7125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7126" type="x-p"/> He will not fail thee - Thy expectation, however strong and extensive, shall never be disappointed: thou canst not expect too much from him. <div eID="gen7126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7127" type="x-p"/> Neither forsake thee - He knows that without him thou canst do nothing, and therefore he will continue with thee, and in such a manner too that the excellence of the power shall appear to be of him, and not of man.
entries.80bbd6ef06d73c20df0c959c13700f5c89a03682: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen7127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7128" type="x-p"/> Moses wrote this law - Not the whole Pentateuch, but either the discourses and precepts mentioned in the preceding chapters, or the book of Deuteronomy, which is most likely. <div eID="gen7128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7129" type="x-p"/> Some of the rabbins have pretended that Moses wrote thirteen copies of the whole Pentateuch; that he gave one to each of the twelve tribes, and the thirteenth was laid up by the ark. This opinion deserves little credit. Some think that he wrote two copies, one of which he gave to the priests and Levites for general use, according to what is said in this verse, the other to be laid up beside the ark as a standard copy for reference, and to be a witness against the people should they break it or become idolatrous. This second copy is supposed to be intended <reference osisRef="Deu.31.26">Deu 31:26</reference>. As the law was properly a covenant or contract between God and the people, it is natural to suppose there were two copies of it, that each of the contracting parties might have one: therefore one was laid up beside the ark, this was the Lord's copy; another was given to the priests and Levites, this was the people's copy.
entries.6eb04fde414a2c85af3cd74aa49cbefa1d9d268e: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen7129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7130" type="x-p"/> At the end of every seven years - thou shalt read this law - Every seventh year was a year of release, <reference osisRef="Deu.15.1">Deu 15:1</reference>, at which time the people's minds, being under a peculiar degree of solemnity, were better disposed to hear and profit by the words of God. I suppose on this ground also that the whole book of Deuteronomy is meant, as it alone contains an epitome of the whole Pentateuch. And in this way some of the chief Jewish rabbins understand this place. <div eID="gen7130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7131" type="x-p"/> It is strange that this commandment, relative to a public reading of the law every seven years, should have been rarely attended to. It does not appear that from the time mentioned <reference osisRef="Jos.8.30">Jos 8:30</reference>, at which time this public reading first took place, till the reign of Jehoshaphat <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.7">2Chr 17:7</reference>, there was any public seventh year reading - a period of 530 years. The next seventh year reading was not till the eighteenth year of the reign of Josiah, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.30">2Chr 34:30</reference>, a space of two hundred and eighty-two years. Nor do we find any other publicly mentioned from this time till the return from the Babylonish captivity, <reference osisRef="Neh.8.2">Neh 8:2</reference>. Nor is there any other on record from that time to the destruction of Jerusalem. See Dodd.
entries.7f0de33a1365245c45fa3bf61f89c87a64bbb3ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen7131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7132" type="x-p"/> Behold, thou shalt sleep with thy fathers - שכב shocheb, thou shalt lie down; it signifies to rest, take rest in sleep, and, metaphorically, to die. Much stress cannot be safely laid on this expression to prove the immortality of the soul, or that the people in the time of Moses had a distinct notion of its separate existence. It was, however, understood in this sense by Jonathan ben Uzziel, who in his Targum paraphrases the word thus: "Thou shalt lie down in the dust with thy fathers; and thy soul (נשמתך nishmethach) shall be laid up in the treasury of the life to come with thy fathers."
entries.dccaab2d7b511172e790d90fed66f60ff01c199d: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen7132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7133" type="x-p"/> I will surely hide my face - Withdraw my approbation and my protection. This is a general meaning of the word in Scripture.
entries.e2728e9b3ccb5be1f8141d390fb7e5cf8de55afb: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen7133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7134" type="x-p"/> Write ye this song - The song which follows in the next chapter. Things which were of great importance and of common concern were, among the ancients, put into verse, as this was found the best method of keeping them in remembrance, especially in those times when writing was little practiced. Even prose was sometimes sung. The history of Herodotus was divided into Nine books, and each inscribed with the name of one of the Nine Muses, because these books were anciently sung. Homer is reported to have sung his poems through different Greek cities. Aristotle observes that anciently the people sung their laws. And Cicero observes that it was a custom among the ancient Romans to sing the praises of their heroes at the public festivals. This was the case among the northern inhabitants of Europe, particularly in Ireland and Scotland; hence the Gaelic poetry of Ossian and others. See Dodd; and see the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.15.1">Exo 15:1</reference>, where the subject is largely treated.
entries.d41b27f83be3c2465aa8bb1d5929966a71789104: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen7134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7135" type="x-p"/> This song shall testify against them - Because in it their general defection is predicted, but in such a way as to show them how to avoid the evil; and if they did not avoid the evil, and the threatened punishment should come upon them, then the song should testify against them, by showing that they had been sufficiently warned, and might have lived to God, and so escaped those disasters.
entries.0a70097043b4189990bde2c51ae46e0d0dbde2da: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen7135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7136" type="x-p"/> Take this book of the law - The standard copy to which all transcripts must ultimately refer: another copy was put into the bands of the priests. See the note on <reference osisRef="Deu.31.9">Deu 31:9</reference>.
entries.b2dd5d90b948d217d10e03044b05ba20a81caec9: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen7136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7137" type="x-p"/> While I am yet alive - ye have been rebellious - Such was the disposition of this people to act contrary to moral goodness that Moses felt himself justified in inferring what would take place from what had already happened. <div eID="gen7137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7138" type="x-p"/> 1. Never was a people more fully and faithfully warned, and from this very circumstance we may see that they were under no fatal constraining necessity to commit sin against God; they might have avoided it, but they would not. God was present to help them, till by their repeated provocations they forced him to depart: wrath therefore came upon them to the uttermost because they sinned when they might have lived to the glory of God. Those who abuse God's grace shall not only have that grace taken away from them, but shall be punished for the abuse of it, as well as for the transgression. Every sin is double, and must have a twofold punishment; for 1. Grace is resisted; 2. Transgression is committed; and God will visit for both. <div eID="gen7138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7139" type="x-p"/> 2. How astonishing it is that, with such examples of God's justice before their eyes, the Jews should be so little affected; and that the Gentiles, who have received the Gospel of God, should act as if God would no more punish transgression, or that he must be so partial to them as to pass by iniquities for which the hand of his justice still continues heavy upon the descendants of Jacob! Let them take heed, for if God spared not the natural branches, he will not spare them. If they sin after the manner of the Jews, they may expect to be partakers with them in their punishments. What God does to nations he will do to individuals who reject his mercy, or trample under foot his grace; the soul that sinneth, and returns not to God by repentance and faith, shall die. This is a decree of God that shall never be reversed, and every day bears witness how strictly he keeps it in view. <div eID="gen7139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7140" type="x-p"/> 3. The ode composed by Moses for this occasion was probably set to some lively and affecting air, and sung by the people. It would be much easier to keep such a song in remembrance, than an equal quantity of prose. The whole would have the additional circumstances of cadence and tune to cause it to be often repeated; and thus insure its being kept in memory. Poetry, though often, nay, generally abused, is nevertheless a gift from God, and may be employed with the best effect in his service. A very considerable part of the Old Testament is written in poetry; particularly the whole book of Psalms, great part of the prophet Isaiah, the Lamentations, and much of the minor prophets. Those who speak against poetic compositions in the service of God, speak against what they do not understand. All that a man hath should be consecrated to his Maker, and employed in his service; not only the energy of his heart and mind, the physical force of his body, but also the musical tones and modulations of his voice.  <chapter eID="Deut.31"/> <div eID="gen7140" type="x-p"/>

entries.f238480f2e1c57935ed585fe30e3dc8fa622d29b: <div eID="gen2546" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">IV. Moses’ Farewell and Death - Deuteronomy 31-34</title> <div sID="gen2547" type="x-p"/> With the renewal of the covenant, by the choice set before the people between blessing and curse, life and death, Moses had finished the interpretation and enforcement of the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.1.5">Deu 1:5</reference>), and brought the work of legislation to a close. But in order that the work to which the Lord had called him might be thoroughly completed, it still remained for him, before his approaching death, to hand over the task of leading the people into Canaan to Joshua, who had been appointed as his successor, to finish writing out the laws, and to hand over the book of the law to the priests. The Lord also directed him to write an ode, as a witness against the people, on account of their obstinacy, and teach it to the Israelites. To these last arrangements and acts of Moses, which are narrated in ch. 31 and 32, there are added in ch. 33 the blessing with which this man of god bade farewell to the tribes of Israel, and in ch. 34 the account of his death, with which the Pentateuch closes. <div eID="gen2547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2548" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Deut.31.1-Deut.31.13">Deu 31:1-13</reference> describe how Moses promised the help of the Lord in the conquest of the land, both to the people generally, and also to Joshua, their leader into Canaan (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.2-Deut.31.8">Deu 31:2-8</reference>), and commanded the priests to keep the book of the law, and read it publicly every seventh year (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.9-Deut.31.13">Deu 31:9-13</reference>); and <reference osisRef="Deut.31.14-Deut.31.23">Deu 31:14-23</reference>, how the Lord appeared to Moses before the tabernacle, and directed him to compose an ode as a testimony against the apostasy of the people, and promised Joshua His assistance. And lastly, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.24-Deut.31.27">Deu 31:24-27</reference> relate how the book of the law, when brought to completion, was handed over to the Levites; and <reference osisRef="Deut.31.28-Deut.31.30">Deu 31:28-30</reference> describe the reading of the ode to the people. <div eID="gen2548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2549" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Deut.31.1">Deu 31:1</reference> Moses’ final arrangements are announced. ויּלך does not mean “he went away” (into his tent), which does not tally with what follows (“and spake”); nor is it merely equivalent to <hi type="italic">porro</hi>, <hi type="italic">amplius</hi>. It serves, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.2.1">Exo 2:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.35.22">Gen 35:22</reference>, as a pictorial description of what he was about to do, in the sense of “he prepared himself,” or rose up. After closing the exposition of the law, Moses had either withdrawn, or at any rate made a pause, before he proceeded to make his final arrangements for laying down his office, and taking leave of the people.
entries.cd4b898b98604d99c376915c99d146fd310b9c33: <reference osisRef="Deut.31.2">Deu 31:2</reference> <div eID="gen2549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2550" type="x-p"/> These last arrangements he commences with the declaration, that he must now bid them farewell, as he is 120 years old (which agrees with <reference osisRef="Exod.7.7">Exo 7:7</reference>), and can no more go out and in, i.e., no longer work in the nation and for it (see at Num 27:17); and the Lord has forbidden him to cross over the Jordan and enter Canaan (see Num 20:24). The first of these reasons is not at variance with the statement in <reference osisRef="Deut.34.7">Deu 34:7</reference>, that up to the time of his death his eyes were not dim, nor his strength abated. For this is merely an affirmation, that he retained the ability to see and to work to the last moment of his life, which by no means precludes his noticing the decline of his strength, and feeling the approach of his death.
entries.e8eee0a658f95cc7a60a2412ad153f79260a9f40: <reference osisRef="Deut.31.3-Deut.31.5">Deu 31:3-5</reference> <div eID="gen2550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2551" type="x-p"/> But although Moses could not, and was not to lead his people into Canaan, the Lord would fulfil His promise, to go before Israel and destroy the Canaanites, like the two kings of the Amorites; only they (the Israelites) were to do to them as the Lord had commanded them, i.e., to root out the Canaanites (vid., Deu 7:2.; Num 33:51.; Exo 34:11.).
entries.ffbce88255a481f9d47afec9234080b3c312876b: <reference osisRef="Deut.31.6">Deu 31:6</reference> <div eID="gen2551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2552" type="x-p"/> Israel was therefore to be of good courage, and not to be afraid of them (vid., <reference osisRef="Deut.1.21">Deu 1:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.20.3">Deu 20:3</reference>).
entries.b61c0861d795391764e0e3269d2608943c71f510: <reference osisRef="Deut.31.7-Deut.31.8">Deu 31:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen2552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2553" type="x-p"/> Moses then encourages Joshua in the same way in the presence of all the people, on the strength of the promise of God in <reference osisRef="Deut.1.38">Deu 1:38</reference> and Num 27:18. את־העם תּבוא, “<hi type="italic">thou wilt come with this people into the land</hi>.” These words are quite appropriate; and the alteration of תּבוא into תּביא, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.31.23">Deu 31:23</reference> (<hi type="italic">Samar</hi>., <hi type="italic">Syr</hi>., <hi type="italic">Vulg</hi>.), is a perfectly unnecessary conjecture; for Joshua was not appointed leader of the people here, but simply promised an entrance with all the people into Canaan.
entries.fdffe9acbde5cceae0bea35078a5ab9d10ae2d58: <reference osisRef="Deut.31.9-Deut.31.13">Deu 31:9-13</reference> <div eID="gen2553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2554" type="x-p"/> Moses then handed over the law which he had written to the Levitical priests who carried the ark of the covenant, and to all the elders of Israel, with instructions to read it to the people at the end of every seven years, during the festal season of the year of release (“at the end,” as in <reference osisRef="Deut.15.1">Deu 15:1</reference>), viz., at the fast of Tabernacles (see <reference osisRef="Lev.23.34">Lev 23:34</reference>), when they appeared before the Lord. It is evident from the context and contents of these verses, apart from <reference osisRef="Deut.31.24">Deu 31:24</reference>, that the ninth verse is to be understood in the way described, i.e., that the two clauses, which are connected together by <hi type="italic">vav. relat.</hi> (“<hi type="italic">and Moses wrote this law</hi>,” “<hi type="italic">and delivered it</hi>”), are not logically co-ordinate, but that the handing over of the written law was the main thing to be recorded here. With regard to the handing over of the law, the fact that Moses not only gave the written law to the priests, that they might place it by the ark of the covenant, but also “<hi type="italic">to all the elders of Israel</hi>,” proves clearly enough that Moses did not intend at this time to give the law-book entirely out of his own hands, but that this handing over was merely an assignment of the law to the persons who were to take care, that in the future the written law should be kept before the people, as the rule of their life and conduct, and publicly read to them. The explanation which <hi type="italic">J. H. Mich. </hi>gives is perfectly correct, “He gave it for them to teach and keep.” The law-book would only have been given to the priests, if the object had been simply that it should be placed by the ark of the covenant, or at the most, in the presence of the elders, but certainly not <hi type="italic">to</hi> all the elders, since they were not allowed to touch the ark. The correctness of this view is placed beyond all doubt by the contents of Deu 31:10. The main point in hand was not the writing out of the law, or the transfer of it to the priests and elders of the nation, but the command to read the law in the presence of the people at the feast of Tabernacles of the year of release. The writing out and handing over simply formed the substratum for this command, so that we cannot infer from them, that by this act Moses formally gave the law out of his own hands. He entrusted the reading to the priesthood and the college of elders, as the spiritual and secular rulers of the congregation; and hence the singular, “Thou shalt read this law to all Israel.” The regulations as to the persons who were to undertake the reading, and also as to the particular time during the seven days’ feast, and the portions that were to be read, he left to the rulers of the congregation. We learn from <reference osisRef="Neh.8.18">Neh 8:18</reference>, that in Ezra’s time they read <hi type="italic">in</hi> the book of the law every day from the first to the last day of the feast, from which we may see on the one hand, that the whole of the <hi type="italic">Thorah</hi> (or Pentateuch), from beginning to end, was not read; and on the other hand, by comparing the expression in <reference osisRef="Deut.31.18">Deu 31:18</reference>, “the book of the law of God,” with “the law,” in <reference osisRef="Deut.31.14">Deu 31:14</reference>, that the reading was not restricted to Deuteronomy: for, according to v. 14, they had already been reading in Leviticus (ch. 23) before the feast was held - an evident proof that Ezra the scribe did not regard the book of Deuteronomy like the critics of our day, as the true national law-book, an acquaintance with which was all that the people required. Moses did not fix upon the feast of Tabernacles of the sabbatical year as the time for reading the law, because it fell at the beginning of the year,<note placement="foot">It by no means follows, that because the sabbatical year commenced with the omission of the usual sowing, i.e., began in the autumn with the civil year, it therefore commenced with the feast of Tabernacles, and the order of the feasts was reversed in the sabbatical year. According to <reference osisRef="Exod.23.16">Exo 23:16</reference>, the feast of Tabernacles did not fall at the beginning, but at the end of the civil year. The commencement of the year with the first of <hi type="italic">Tisri</hi> was an arrangement introduced after the captivity, which the Jews had probably adopted from the Syrians (see my <hi type="italic">bibl. Archaeol.</hi> i. §74, note 15). Nor does it follow, that because the year of jubilee was to be proclaimed on the day of atonement in the sabbatical year with a blast of trumpets (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.9">Lev 25:9</reference>), therefore the year of jubilee must have begun with the feast of Tabernacles. The proclamation of festivals is generally made some time before they commence.</note> as <hi type="italic">Schultz</hi> wrongly supposes, that the people might thereby be incited to occupy this year of entire rest in holy employment with the word and works of God. And the reading itself was nether intended to promote a more general acquaintance with the law on the part of the people, - an object which could not possibly have been secured by reading it once in seven years; nor was it merely to be a solemn promulgation and restoration of the law as the rule for the national life, for the purpose of removing any irregularities that might have found their way in the course of time into either the religious or the political life of the nation (Bähr, Symbol. ii. p. 603). To answer this end, it should have been connected with the Passover, the festival of Israel’s birth. The reading stood rather in close connection with the idea of the festival itself; it was intended to quicken the soul with the law of the Lord, to refresh the heart, to enlighten the eyes, - in short, to offer the congregation the blessing of the law, which David celebrated from his own experience in Ps. 19:8-15, to make the law beloved and prized by the whole nation, as a precious gift of the grace of God. Consequently (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.12">Deu 31:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.13">Deu 31:13</reference>), not only the men, but the women and children also, were to be gathered together for this purpose, that they might hear the word of God, and learn to fear the Lord their God, as long as they should live in the land which He gave them for a possession. On <reference osisRef="Deut.31.11">Deu 31:11</reference>, see <reference osisRef="Exod.23.17">Exo 23:17</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Exod.34.23-Exod.34.24">Exo 34:23-24</reference>, where we also find לראות for להראות (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.24">Exo 34:24</reference>).
entries.3b8b03bb9c00affd7502aaf7134858233211a1fe: <reference osisRef="Deut.31.14-Deut.31.18">Deu 31:14-18</reference> <div eID="gen2554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2555" type="x-p"/> After handing over the office to Joshua, and the law to the priests and elders, Moses was called by the Lord to come to the tabernacle with Joshua, to command him (צוּה), i.e., to appoint him, confirm him in his office. To this end the Lord appeared in the tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.15">Deu 31:15</reference>), in a pillar of cloud, which remained standing before it, as in Num 12:5 (see the exposition of Num 11:25). But before appointing Joshua, He announced to Moses that after his death the nation would go a whoring after other gods, and would break the covenant, for which it would be visited with severe afflictions, and directed him to write an ode and teach it to the children of Israel, that when the apostasy should take place, and punishment from God be felt in consequence, it might speak as a witness against the people, as it would not vanish from their memory. The Lord communicated this commission to Moses in the presence of Joshua, that he also might hear from the mouth of God that the Lord foreknew the future apostasy of the people, and yet nevertheless would bring them into the promised land. In this there was also implied an admonition to Joshua, not only to take care that the Israelites learned the ode and kept it in their memories, but also to strive with all his might to prevent the apostasy, so long as he was leader of Israel; which Joshua did most faithfully to the very end of his life (vid., Josh 23 and 24). - The announcement of the falling away of the Israelites from the Lord into idolatry, and the burning of the wrath of God in consequence (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.16-Deut.31.18">Deu 31:16-18</reference>), serves as a basis for the command in Deu 31:19. In this announcement the different points are simply linked together with “and,” whereas in their actual signification they are subordinate to one another: When thou shalt lie with thy fathers, and the people shall rise up, and go a whoring after other gods: My anger will burn against them, etc. קוּם, to rise up, to prepare, serves to bring out distinctly the course which the thing would take. The expression, “<hi type="italic">foreign gods of the land</hi>,” indicates that in the land which Jehovah gave His people, He (Jehovah) alone was God and Lord, and that He alone was to be worshipped there. בּקרבּו is in apposition to שׁמּה, “<hi type="italic">whither thou comest, in the midst of it</hi>.” The punishment announced in <reference osisRef="Deut.31.17">Deu 31:17</reference> corresponds most closely to the sin of the nation. For going a whoring after strange gods, the anger of the Lord would burn against them; for forsaking Him, He would forsake them; and for breaking His covenant, He would hide His face from them, i.e., withdraw His favour from them, so that they would be destroyed. לאכל היה, it (the nation) will be for devouring, i.e., will be devoured or destroyed (see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §237, <hi type="italic">c</hi>.; and on אכל in this sense, see <reference osisRef="Deut.7.16">Deu 7:16</reference>, and Num 14:9). “<hi type="italic">And many evils and troubles will befall it; and it will say in that day, Do not these evils befall me, because my God is not in the midst of me?</hi>” When the evils and troubles broke in upon the nation, the people would inquire the cause, and would find it in the fact that they were forsaken by their God; but the Lord (“but I” in <reference osisRef="Deut.31.18">Deu 31:18</reference> forms the antithesis to “they” in <reference osisRef="Deut.31.17">Deu 31:17</reference>) would still hide His face, namely, because simply missing God is not true repentance.
entries.c6758a2c5354d897391ccfa4738cbfe71e107a29: <reference osisRef="Deut.31.19-Deut.31.23">Deu 31:19-23</reference> <div eID="gen2555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2556" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And now</hi>,” sc., because what was announced in <reference osisRef="Deut.31.16-Deut.31.18">Deu 31:16-18</reference> would take place, “<hi type="italic">write you this song</hi>.” “This” refers to the song which follows in ch. 32. Moses and Joshua were to write the song, because they were both of them to strive to prevent the apostasy of the people; and Moses, as the author, was to teach it to the children of Israel, to make them learn it, that it might be a witness for the Lord (for Me) against the children of Israel. “This” is defined still further in <reference osisRef="Deut.31.20">Deu 31:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.21">Deu 31:21</reference> : if Israel, through growing satisfied and fat in its land, which was so rich in costly good, should turn to other gods, and the Lord should visit it in consequence with grievous evils and troubles, the song was to answer before Israel as a witness; i.e., not only serve the Lord as a witness to the people that He had foretold all the evil consequences of apostasy, and had given Israel proper warning (<hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>), but to serve, as we may see from <reference osisRef="Deut.31.20">Deu 31:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.21">Deu 31:21</reference>, and from the contents of the song, as a witness, on the one hand, that the Lord had conferred upon the people so many benefits and bestowed upon them such abundant blessings of His grace, that apostasy from Him was the basest ingratitude, for which they would justly be punished; and, on the other hand, that the Lord had not rejected His people in spite of the punishments inflicted upon them, but would once more have compassion upon them and requite their foes, and thus would sanctify and glorify Himself as the only true God by His judgments upon Israel and the nations. The law, with its commandments, promises, and threats, was already a witness of this kind against Israel (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.31.26">Deu 31:26</reference>); but just as in every other instance the appearance of a plurality of unanimous witnesses raises the matter into an indisputable truth, so the Lord would set up another witness against the Israelites besides the law, in the form of this song, which was adapted to give all the louder warning, “because the song would not be forgotten out of the mouths of their seed” (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.21">Deu 31:21</reference>). The song, when once it had passed into the mouths of the people, would not very readily vanish from their memory, but would be transmitted from generation to generation, and be heard from the mouths of their descendants, as a perpetual warning voice, as it would be used by Israel for God knew the invention of the people, i.e., the thoughts and purposes of their heart, which they cherished (עשׂה used to denote the doing of the heart, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.32.6">Isa 32:6</reference>) even then before He had brought them into Canaan. (On <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Deut.31.20">Deu 31:20</reference></hi>, vid., <reference osisRef="Deut.7.5">Deu 7:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.9.5">Deu 9:5</reference>, and Exo 3:8.) - In <reference osisRef="Deut.31.22">Deu 31:22</reference> the result is anticipated, and the command of God is followed immediately by an account of its completion by Moses (just as in <reference osisRef="Exod.12.50">Exo 12:50</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.16.34">Lev 16:34</reference>, etc.). - After this command with reference to the song, the Lord appointed Joshua to the office which he had been commanded to take, urging him at the same time to be courageous, and promising him His help in the conquest of Canaan. That the subject to ויצו is not Moses, but Jehovah, is evident partly from the words themselves, “I will be with thee' (vid., <reference osisRef="Exod.3.12">Exo 3:12</reference>). (Note: <hi type="italic">Knobel's</hi> assertion (on Num 27:23) that the appointment of Joshua on the part of Moses by the imposition of hands, as described in that passage, is at variance with this verse, scarcely needs any refutation. Or is it really the case, that the installation of Joshua on the part of God is irreconcilable with his ordination by Moses?)
entries.8d05bc6276d74aba5463e2958a3dc6cf21132785: <reference osisRef="Deut.31.24-Deut.31.27">Deu 31:24-27</reference> <div eID="gen2556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2557" type="x-p"/> With the installation of Joshua on the part of God, the official life of Moses was brought to a close.
